utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The parties may have noticed that I did not give the usual instruction at the end of yesterday's session to the witness. Immediately after court I asked Mr. Registrar to convey this same instruction to the witness. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it was conveyed to us by Mr. Monkhouse and everything is fine as far as the Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to that, of course, our position is the same, Your Honour. I just wanted to bring to the Court's attention, since it was raised yesterday, the matter of the review of the six audio clips that were played. As it turns out there are not -- at least as I now understand it, full transcripts available for those or anything approaching full transcripts available for those audiotapes. They constitute a total of in excess of six hours, so I was unable to review them and it will obviously take some time to do so. I don't anticipate, as I think yesterday, there will be any objection to the excerpts themselves but of course the Prosecution wishes to have an opportunity to review the entirety of the transcripts to see if the additional portions need to be admitted. So I think given the length of those transcripts of the audiotapes, I would ask for a week to -- or so to look them over. I mean, I will not be able to do that today, obviously, or approach completing it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will see what the possible consequences are because, of course, I'm aware that if any other portions of those audiotapes would need attention, then of course the witness has gone by then. We'll then consider what to do understand those circumstances, whether there would be any need to recall the witness. I'm not suggesting to do that. But, at the same time, we'll have to see what happens, what the positions of the Prosecution will be, and then we'll act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may. I -- we have no objection to that, to let them review the audios, obviously. If I can just clarify I -- then obviously misunderstood what I was being asked yesterday. I thought I was being asked if the actual portions that we were playing had been transcribed not that we had, as he said, six hours of audio. We obviously don't have the resources to transcribe audio, particularly audio that we aren't going to use in Court. Our procedure essentially was what we do with videos, for example, if we cut a certain portion of what is an otherwise a longer video we, I think, have reached an agreement with the Mr. Tieger that we will present the audio -- short clip and then give them the complete raw footage, for example, so that they have the entire material which is how I was proceeding yesterday was to give them the whole audio but to transcribe the actual portion used in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that. Of course, we should needless transcribing. Perhaps, Mr. Tieger, if you could work on the basis of the video and the audio material without transcripts to start with and then to see whether the context reveals any important issues which should be dealt with. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then once the witness is in, you can start using your one hour and seven minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Galbraith. I'd like to remind you, as I did yesterday, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony and Mr. Kehoe will now continue his cross-examination. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I would like to shift subjects for one moment -- for a few moments if I may and show you a few documents and then ask you a few questions about them. This relates to a normalisation agreement between the FRY and the Republic of Croatia and if I could bring up 1D33-0199 first. As it states on the front page this is a letter dated September 11th, 1996, from the permanent representative of Croatia to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General, and it's signed by Mario Nobilo, Ambassador, permanent representative, and has to do with the agreement on normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. If we could turn to the next page, it begins with the agreement itself. And if we could go to yet the next page and focus on the Article 7, and Mr. Ambassador I'm not going to read the whole thing, but if at any moment, Mr. Ambassador, you want to stop and read one particular portion please let me know. Article 7, paragraph 1: "The contracting parties shall ensure conditions for the free and safe return of refugees and displaced persons to their places of residence or other places and that they -- that they freely choose. The contracting parties shall ensure to these persons the return of their property or a adjust compensation. "2. The contracting parties shall ensure full security to the refugees and displaced persons who return. The contracting party the shall assist these persons to ensure the necessary conditions for a normal and safe life. "3. The contracting parties shall declare a general amnesty for all acts committed in connection with the armed conflicts except for the gravest violations of humanitarian law having a nature of war crimes." And if we can just follow up two more pages to the back of the signature page. It is signed in Belgrade on 23 August 1996 by Mate Granic for the Republic of Croatia and Milan Milutinovic for the Republic of Yugoslavia. If we could move to one more document, Mr. Ambassador, before we ask a few questions in this regard. I would like to bring up 1D33-0458. If you can blow that up a bit. This is an Article by Chris Hedges of the New York times, 24 August 1996, and it discusses your comments, Mr. Ambassador, at the middle of the page. You can see the middle of the page beginning with: "This is a historic development said American ambassador to Croatia Peter W. Galbraith, the Serb-Croat conflict was" --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was -- oh, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's in the middle of the page, I apologise. It's four lines down, four paragraphs down. Are you with me sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. "Serb-Croat conflict was at the root of the war in the former Yugoslavia, normalisation of relations between the two largest countries that emerged from the former Yugoslavia is a significant factor in the effort to achieve regional stability." Moving to the bottom of that page, there's another comment by you, Mr. Ambassador. The last line. It says: "There is lot in here that is good for the ordinary Serb," said Mr. Galbraith." Mr. Ambassador, just taking these two documents together, can you discuss the process that went into the Republic of Croatia and Yugoslavia entering into this accord?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place after the Erdut and Dayton peace agreement and both countries had an interest in normalisation of relations, including establishment of normal trade relations, so I think that is the background to it. On the issue of the return of refugees the commitment and compensation, obviously there would have been political pressure in Yugoslavia to accomplish that, but I would say very significantly in Croatia's -- in Tudjman's decision to agree to return of refugees on paper was the very intense pressure that the United States put on Tudjman. We actually imposed sanctions on Croatia and were threatening to cancel the MPRI licence, which was very important to them, unless they agreed to the return of refugees and to the right of these Croatian citizens as we saw them, to get their citizenship and to recover their property. So in effect on that point which is one you were drawing attention to the agreement with Yugoslavia was doing something -- was not a concession as part of that process but something that Croatia had been forced to do particularly by United States pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And United States pressure, did that this also include this -- this amnesty provision that is set forth in paragraph 3, this general amnesty that we just discussed for all acts committed in connection with the armed conflict except for the gravest violations of international humanitarian law having the nature of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amnesty was one of the things that we wanted to see for a number of reasons. First, it was essential to the implementation of the Erdut Agreement, because the idea behind the Erdut Agreement it was that the territory would change hands from Serbian control to being a normal part of Croatia but where the Serb population would remain. But if many of the men there could be indicted for rebellion or treason or a range of other maybe more, you know, smaller crimes, then they would leave and also people who may have committed these crimes would not be able to return. So that was -- certainly there was a very strong desire on our part that crimes like treason and amnesty -- that there be an amnesty for crimes like treason, rebellion against the Croatian state, which incidentally is normal in many cases when wars end. We were against amnesty in for war crimes and serious crimes like murder and rape. And with regard to war crimes we -- we believed and insisted that what we called the rules of the road would apply; namely, that if there was somebody who was accused of a war crime, that case would be referred to this Court which would then make a determination as to whether was there prima facie case of it being a war crime, possibly take jurisdiction here, and if they didn't and if they agreed that it was a war crime, then it could be prosecuted domestically in either Croatia. The same rules applied to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Ambassador, just take a little break. I may just discuss a couple of elements of your statement, the first being that, and correct me if I'm wrong, it was never contemplated there would be an amnesty for murders or rapes?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not -- we the United States did not support an amnesty for murders or rapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. But for lower-level crimes or in addition -- lower-level crimes with charging people coming back with burning or looting, those are the types of crimes that you wanted an amnesty?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually remember our position on those crimes. What I remember us being most focussed on was an amnesty for treason, rebellion, those bigger crimes, and maybe some smaller crimes, but I don't know -- I can't remember what position we might have taken on arson, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ultimately, even with regard to war crimes, the United States and the UN put pressure on Croatia to limit the prosecution of Serbs coming back for war crimes to 25 people, did they not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. What I recall frankly were the rules of the road; namely, that if somebody was to be charged with war crimes it would be referred to this Tribunal which would make a determination and then there could either be prosecution here or domestically. I don't recall any notion of limiting it to numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't recall any number of 25 at all?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But this amnesty law was designed to cover, barring serious war crimes, was designed to cover all the people in the former Yugoslavia and the Republic of Croatia for particular crimes as set forth in the agreement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring now to the Croatia-Yugoslavia agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, in paragraph 3 it was a general amnesty for everybody.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that would have been an a bi-lateral agreement but it wouldn't have actually implemented the amnesty. That would have required, presumably, separate domestic legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But as far as the two countries were concerned, it was covering everybody, that was what was contemplated? As we can see in the paragraph there is no distinction between Serb or Croat or Muslim. It says a general amnesty.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back and look at that specific paragraph again. I mean, did I read it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can return back. It is 1D33-0199. If we could go to Article 7, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see that, sir, it is just a general amnesty?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer into evidence 1D33-0199 and 1D33-0458.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D33-0199 becomes Exhibit D412. And 1D33-0458 becomes Exhibit D413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D412 and D413 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before I make one comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, there was a degree of pressure and you mentioned a degree of pressure from the United States but also from the international community to pass this amnesty law, was there not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we worked closely with our European allies and the Russians and United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a degree of documents that we'll pass across the bar table, and naturally we'll give it to our colleagues across the bar, concerning various international documents requesting that this amnesty -- this amnesty law be passed. Of course, we won't take up the time to go through it right now, but we will pass that there, basically UN documents and UN Security Council documents so we can move on to another subject, but I will consult with my colleague, Mr. Tieger, before we pass those across the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll hear from Mr. Tieger whether there are any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I would like to talk to you just a few brief moments. In paragraph 33, you are talking -- paragraph 33 of your statement, if you will. In paragraph 33, you note -- I'm sorry, sir, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "After the flight in August of Krajina Serbs, however, President Tudjman was very much focussed and very clear that they should not come back. He explained that the Serbs had opted out of being Croats and that he had offered them a chance to stay and they left. Croatia could not take this disloyal group back into the heart of Croatia." Now, right after the Krajina war I think we talked yesterday about the continuation of the war from August into September and October, and I would like to present a document which is 1D33-0190. And, again, Mr. Ambassador, I just want to show you a series of documents and some other items before we entire into this area if we may?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just comment. There is a typo there in 33. It should say, "They had opted out of being Croatians," not "Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Needless to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Mr. Ambassador, this is a document. It is a directive coming from Milan Martic, dated 4 September 1995, and it is the formation of the RSK liberation army and coalescing into the combat operations in the territory of the Republic of Srpska and the RSK; suffice it to say, it's his order reforming the ARSK to join with the forces of the Bosnian-Serb army, the VRS. I know that you probably haven't seen this document before, sir, I just wanted to bring it to your attention. Before I begin this, I would like to turn to an individual which is 1D330-188. This a clip, Mr. Ambassador, of a movie called "The Fall of Krajina" that was put together in Belgrade in 2006. The movie is called the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last item that I would like to show you before we inquire is one last document which is a seized VRS document, 1D33-0486. It has not yet been released into e-court, so I would ask the Court's indulgence with the court usher if we can hand a hard copy to this document to the witness as well as the Court. It is a four-page document, Your Honours, that has -- Mr. Monkhouse, I believe it's the other document, that is not correct -- we can put it on Sanction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is a document that was seized after the fall of the Krajina, as you can see in the back pages it -- it has a Cyrillic type but it is an RSK document dated 1 January 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, the document I have has no Cyrillic type.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, if you can -- yours is the English. We're just going to deal with the English if you look up the pages you can see the Cyrillic down there but I gave you the translation.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. But you only me the two pages so there is nothing for me to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. This is a document, an ARSK document that notes available personnel for military service according to age and qualification and it notes that the date on the document was 1 January 1995. And we'll just deal with the totals. The total available personnel for military service, they note, various age categories in the first column is 111.031. Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the number of people who were available for military service that had either been available or been in the ARSK, would you agree with me that the Republic of Croatia was right to have certain security concerns in bringing back a group of individuals they had just been fighting against some two months prior. Would you agree that that -- that the Republic of Croatia was right to have those security concerns?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the particular time that -- I'm sure during this document in January, but certainly after the war in the Krajina the war was still going on certainly until sometime in October and thereafter, so during those month the HV forces were continuing to fight with the joint forces of the Bosnian-Serbs and the Krajina-Serbs, were they not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So given the fact that they were still fighting these individuals, is it still your position that the Republic of Croatia should not have had security concerns, just bringing back people without finding out who they were and what they had been doing?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the people who left the Krajina were old, were women, were children, were not combatants, and the Republic of Croatia barred those people from returning, as well as able -- as well as military-aged men. I don't think very many people who were intending to engage in combat against Croatia would in fact have returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, then where did the 111.000 people available for military service go?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm having some difficulty myself parsing through this particular document in identifying precisely what it is supposed to indicate. It was indicated as an ARSK document. It is the not clear it me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it Mr. Kehoe said an RSK not ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And so I guess I'm only concerned then about any conflation between the forces of the RSK and the former forces of the ARSK in questions relate to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question - and pardon me if I have conflated ideas here and I try to parse it more finely - but as of January 1995 this document reflects 111.000 individuals available for military service. And the issue is if in fact a large percentage of the people left the Krajina, where did these 111 [sic] people who were available for military service go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, and maybe it is my problem, but as I understand the question, it -- it assumes that 111.000 of the people who left were those available for military service, and I can't find the basis for that in this particular document, which I understand is an RSK document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's try to get matters straight. It appears that on the 1st of January, 1995, the RSK considered 111.000 people available for military service. Among them 26.000 over 45 years of age; 8.000 up to 22 years of age. The whole range we find in here. Now, the question where they would go, Mr. Kehoe, shouldn't we first establish whether there's any knowledge on, first of all, whether all these 111.000 would go, but also where they came from. I mean, they could have been in barracks; they could have been farming; they could have been in the industry; they -- so it's a very general question, and it is a hypothetical question, very much. So before we put this question to Mr. Galbraith, I think we should further explore what we know about these people. For example, how many of the 111.000 were already engaged in military activities, perhaps all of them, or just all being available; whether where they came from. We have heard evidence that there was a general call for mobilisation. We also know that a lot of people were still on their farms. So, therefore, to say where should they go or where would they go is of a high hypothetical nature, and I think Mr. Galbraith should be in a position to tell us what he knows about it and whether he has ever developed any thoughts on this issue, rather than to put this question to him now. I don't know whether it comes as a comprise to Mr. Galbraith or whether he has given thorough thought to this question. Let's hear from Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the first point I'd make is that this actually provides some interesting data in connection with the question you asked at the end of the session yesterday about the population, because if you look at this document, first, we need to subtract -- let's look at the total on the upper left-hand corner, 111.000. We immediately need to subtract the Vukovar total, 41.000, because that is in eastern Slavonia, obviously those people didn't leave. So we're talking about 70.000 men in the age range -- well, of -- what would be remotely described as military. I don't know what the phrase "up to 22 means." I presume that that's not counting infants, male infants, but anyhow. So, first, it would suggest that the -- if there are 70.000 men of military age in the Krajina, that the population that left would be in the range not of 100.000 but maybe in the range of 200.000. We believed it was probably about 180.000. Second, I have no idea how they're counting people, but it's almost -- I mean, I can't believe that they have 70.000 men under arms, because to have 70.000 men under arms well, first, out of a population of 100.000 which is what Tudjman was saying, would be totally absurd, out of a population of 200.000 would be impossible and it certainly didn't match what we had observed. So in some sense I think the number of troops is probably summed up by the phrase "conscripts and soldiers." And the phrase "reserve soldiers" and "reserve NCOs" may have be anybody who had ever served in the military which I think would be consistent with the Yugoslav system, but that doesn't mean that those people were ever mobilised, ever capable of being mobilised. About this I simply don't know. But surely, surely, many most of what were called reserve soldiers which is the largest category, it's 91.000 out of 111.000, 90 per cent, those reserve soldiers would be men engaged in ordinary civilian occupations, not a military threat to anybody. And I can also tell you from observation that people in the Krajina region, it was a pretty tough existence, so beyond a certain age these guys were not very fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this time I'd like to offer into evidence 1D33-0486.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- I just have a sort of a conditional no objection to that, and simply I just want to consult, I don't have any objection in principle. I would like to consult with my colleagues afterwards just about, I gather this is -- I think it was represented as a captured document, I just want to confirm that with him afterwards. But in principle no objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then have you an opportunity to come back to it. Would that be within the next 24 hours, would that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D414, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't seen the original yet, but, I take it that the original will be uploaded in e-court --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- soon. With the proviso that if the original would show something different or would raise certain questions that they can be raised either by the parties or by the Bench. But as matters stand now, the document, which still needs a number -- no, it is D414 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd also like to tender the Red Berets video 1D33-0188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do have an objection at this point Your Honour, but I'm not -- I haven't had a chance to fully explore that, but I'm not confident that that document relates precisely to the subject matter which was at issue here. So if I could have some period, again 24 hours should be more than sufficient to check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've looked at the video, Mr. Kehoe, is it perfectly clear what we are looking at, who was who? I saw a person clearly visible. Was it about ARSK soldiers returning to, I take it in Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were under -- who were treated in a way where they were not free to decide what they wanted to do and in connection with the document you earlier showed, is it that they were more or less forced to join the armed forces so as to create a joint -- joint armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the video is after Storm Krajina Serbs in Belgrade being rounded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- and then being sent to Erdut in Slavonia to fight against the HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the video in itself says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- it's in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that it was in Belgrade because you said that it was Belgrade television and not that it happened in Belgrade and that these, of course, that happened yesterday a couple of times as well, that the Chamber is not knowing exactly what it is looking at and therefore that is, as far as you understand, what the video shows us and then we have the video itself. 24 hours, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar so the Chamber is in a position to review or reconsider the decision that will be taken now. Mr. Registrar it will would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D415, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes D415 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, the other document is the formation of the ARSK by Mr. Martic dated 4 September 1995, that's 1D33-0190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D416 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber has access to these documents on their computers once they are admitted into evidence or marked for identification. We have no access to the uploaded material which is not yet tendered. So, therefore, in order to be able to go back to these documents because often you used documents in a certain context together with other documents, Chamber would appreciate if you move as quickly as to possible having it assigned a number and at least getting a status so that we can review them by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back, Mr. Ambassador, to compound some of the problems with bringing the refugees back, did you know that the RSK when they left the Krajina took the records with them when they -- and records I'm talking about personnel records, administrative records, and financial records, police records, communication records, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly not aware of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were aware that during this time-frame, at least prior to the normalisation of relations, there was no diplomatic relations and certainly no consular authorities -- the Republic of Croatia did not have any consular authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a liaison office in Zagreb between the two countries. I'm not -- I can't now remember when that was set up, and of course people also had the possibility of trying to get documents in other countries and were never allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the limitations on time we will hand across the bar table the report of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights in Serbia where they discuss the lack of consular authorities in getting proper documentation, but I am limited with time, Mr. Ambassador, so we will hand those across the bar table at the appropriate time? Let me bring a couple of pictures up for you, and if I can get the numbers. First one is 1D33-0436, and if we can go to that one first. And we go to the next one is 1D-- excuse me, before we go to that, you do notice General Gotovina in the centre of that photograph with American army officers, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the picture is not sufficiently good for me to identify people, but if you tell me that's General Gotovina, I'll believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you did know that General Gotovina did attend the International Military and Education Programme in Washington D.C. in September of 1996?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I'm sure I knew that at that time, assuming he attended it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next photograph. That's 1D33-0437. If we can just blow that up a little bit. I'm sure you and I are familiar with that location, General Gotovina being the centre individual in the back. Now, Mr. Ambassador during your term as the ambassador of Croatia, you do know that General Gotovina did go to the United States on three occasions: In September of 1996, April of 1997, and January of 1998. You were aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- again, it's been, you know, many years, so I -- I really can't recall the specifics of it, but what I can tell you is that if General Gotovina went to the United States, and obviously he did, I certainly knew about it, and if he went on a US programme I approved it. With regard to January of 1998, if it was after January 3rd, Ambassador Montgomery was the ambassador. I left that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in any event, taking this yet further, the United States government keeps a list of people who are eligible to come into the United States; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain -- let me take that a little bit further. When a person, such as General Gotovina, asks to come into the United States they request a visa, and in getting that visa coming from Croatia, the United States has a particularly list of people who they will give those visas to and who they will not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain the scenario?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody applies for a visa and then she or he -- application will be considered in compliance with the immigration law which has a number of grounds for exclusion. The most common of which being that we think the person is going to be an intending immigrant. But there are other grounds for exclusion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going into your testimony in the Prlic case, the situation come up with Mr. Mate Boban who was the President of the Herceg-Bosna; do you recall that.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. Boban was not given a visa to come to the United States because he had been entered into the United States visa system as a war criminal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have a list of people we -- that we -- that we permit to come in, but we will have a list of people that we may exclude and the consul general had entered Mr. Boban's name as a person suspected of war crimes, yes, and so on that ground he was excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And by the way, just for frame of reference in the Prlic case, this is page 6525 lines 15 to 20 -- 25. Now, no such limitation had been placed on General Gotovina and no such refusal to allow General Gotovina to come into the United States was ever made, was it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So for 1996, 1997, and I understand you weren't there after 1998, to your knowledge, the United States had never listed General Gotovina as a war criminal in their system, had they?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me talk about a couple of issues as we end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, before I move on to the next subject, and I know my time is very short, consistent with Your Honours' instructions, I would like to move these two photographs into evidence, 1D33-0436 and 1D33-0437.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D33-0436 becomes Exhibit D417; and 1D33-0437 becomes Exhibit D418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D417 and D418 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just intervene I heard Mr. Kehoe was concerned about his time. I have no questions to ask of the witness so it frees the Court timetable somewhat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still to be seen, whether it's -- whether we can compensate between one or the other. The Chamber is not limiting the time because it would not grant sufficient time for cross-examination but, of course, the Chamber looked at how the time was used. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just covering two more topics briefly, Mr. Ambassador, on paragraph 52 -- of your statement, you talk about some looting taking place in Ripac. You say that "I visited Ripac sometimes later perhaps as three weeks afterward." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, I do. I did not mean to imply that the looting took place in Ripac. What I was describing was a trip that went through Ripac from Ripac to Donji Lapac and the looting was in the area between Ripac and Donji Lapac and then in Donji Lapac. Ripac, as I recall, is actually in Bihac, in Bosnia. It's right on the border. So -- and it was under the control of the Bosnian government. So there wouldn't have been looting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with regard to Donji Lapac, you don't know if that was an area that was under the control of General Gotovina and his forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last area. If I can -- and we talked a little bit about the importance of Eastern Slavonia, and you were talking about your efforts to bring Eastern Slavonia -- to reintegrate even Slavonia; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you talked about the fact that Eastern Slavonia was one of the places where people in fact stayed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was -- was that part of the Erdut Agreement that you executed?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me. I apologies.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The verb was wrong, that you assisted and negotiated?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the negotiator of that, the United Nations headed by General Jacques Klein were the executors of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when did that agreement come into effect? When was it signed, better still?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12th November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, sir. That is a -- and it is 1D33-0440. And if we can bring this up. While we're bringing this up, Mr. Ambassador, this is a report of the OSCE mission to the Republic of Croatia on Croatia's progress in meeting international commitments since May 1998, and that document is dated 8 September.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8 September of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, of 1998. Just show the cover page here, sir. And if we can go to page 6 of this document, which is paragraph 23. In paragraph 23, Mr. Ambassador, it notes that "The UNHCR estimates that between August 1996 and July 1998, some 16.000 of the 67.000 Serbs," and let me interject here, my math says that's 24 per cent. "16.000 of the 67.000 Serbs who were residents of the region before the war have left the country mostly to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Available data do not indicate any change in this negative trend since the May Progress Report." Now the Danube is another name for Eastern Slavonia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this document reflects that notwithstanding the agreement that you assisted in bringing about, we still had an exodus of 24 per cent of the Serb population. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that compares to close to 100 per cent from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And despite the end of the war, despite the efforts of your -- that you made to bring back a resolution to this, we still had some 16.000 people leaving as the document reflects, Serbs leaving?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, our position was that people should have a free choice. If they wanted to stay in Croatia, that was their right. If they wanted to leave and another country was prepared to receive them, that was their right. And those that had fled the Krajina should have the right to return home and recover their property. Whether they did or not, frankly that was not our concern. Our concern was simply that refugees have -- every refugee have the right to return. That was a fundamental principle for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer 1D33-0440 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is becomes Exhibit D419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D419 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one last question on this score, Mr. Ambassador. During this time-frame, and we're talking August 1996 to July 1998, this was still an UN-administered area, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The UN administration ran from January of 1996 until January 15th of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So certainly from the beginning of this until six months prior to that it was administered?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: For 18 months of the two-year period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador thank you very much for your time. I appreciate it. Your Honour, I have no further questions. I think my time has expired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You stayed fairly within the time limits I set. I said one hour and seven minutes and that was one hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've got to cut me a little slack here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We understood that the Cermak Defence has no questions. That has not changed meanwhile. Then the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that the Markac Defence asked me if there was a possibility that they will just get a short break while we coordinate here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, I was informed about that. Perhaps we could have an earlier break, so as to make it possible for you. Usually we have a break at 10.30. Let's have an early break and then resume at 25 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith, I wanted to follow up on something that you were discussing towards the end of your testimony with Mr. Kehoe, and that is the issue of return of Serbs from the Krajina and actually from -- whether or not they lived in Krajina. The return of Serbs into Croatia, and it was your testimony that I believe the Croatian government prevented Serbs from returning into the Krajina after Operation Storm. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the most accurate way to say it would be that the Croatian government attempted to make it impossible for Serbs to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: They did in fact return, did they not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few -- well, in the period that we're talking about, very few, eventually and because of US and European pressure, the -- the prohibitions on return and the legal impediments to return were relaxed, more people returned, and then after Tudjman died and a new president and parliament elected, then Croatia's position changed very dramatically and they sought to encourage returns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the issue of return in the period that you say there were few if any returns. What period of time are you talking? Given that Storm might have happened in August of 1995, and your mandate ended in I believe you said January of 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct and in that period there were relatively few returns. There were more in 1997 than in 1996, and that was, again, because of the pressure that we applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to 1D -- I'm sorry, 3D00-1310, please. Actually, let's go -- I'm sorry let's go to 3D00-1306. If we could get that up on the screen, please. And as it's coming up on the screen, I'll represent to you, Ambassador Galbraith, that this is a report written in the year 2000 from the Croatian government, a report that discussed the return of exiles, refugees, and displaced persons into Croatia from those person who had left Croatia. And if we could go -- and I'll represent to you this is just an excerpt, this is a 64-page report in the year 2000, and if we could take a look at the page on the right, if we could enlarge that a little bit or make it full, please. Page 49, we've had translated, talks about a return, and it said in the beginning: "A mass return of Croatian displaced persons began in late summer 1995," which was something that was expected, was it not, Mr. Ambassador, a return of Croats from areas from which they were ethnically cleansed between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was expected and very much desired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If -- I'm pausing here not for dramatic effect but for the translators. If you look at the second paragraph, that begins: "Total return to Croatia," there is, in section 3 of this report, from Autumn 1995 till January 5 of 2000, 41.141 Serbian returnees from Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbian Krajina returned to their homes in Croatia, among which 23.147, a little more than half, came through the implementation of the programme of return, after June 26th of 1998. Now, President Tudjman was president until when?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he died on or about December 14th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So at least as of this document, if you include the year 2000, a year after -- shortly after President Tudjman's death, the report of 41.141 Serbian returnees is given for a total return to Croatia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly wouldn't consider any great significance to it as an indication of Croatia's -- of Croatia's attitude, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nonetheless 41.000 people came back when you said that there were relatively few that came back, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that isn't quite what I said. What I said was that in the period of -- that I was there, well, let be me precise about what I said. What I said was when the Serbs left, Croatia took every legal means possible to prevent their return prohibiting them from citizenship if they did not come back within 30 days and confiscating their property if they did not return in 30 days. Under US pressure that was extended to 90 days. Under US and European pressure, that barrier was -- those prohibitions were eventually lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, I understand that you said that, the numbers here says 41.141 -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is 10 percent relatively few? Is 40 relatively few? Is 70 per cent relatively few? That depends on what you expect and what would be the normally the case. Let's talk about numbers and then we'll -- the Chamber will be able to decide whether it is a few or a lot, and if you insist that Mr. Galbraith answers the questions in the sense of what you apparently consider relatively few, then it's fully understandable that Mr. Galbraith then starts explaining rather than to -- to join or to contradict a judgement -- what would be a judgement of what is relatively few or relatively a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, I'm not trying to get into an argument with you, here. You said that 180.000 Serbs left the -- the Sectors North and South after Operation Storm, roughly, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was that guess based on, by the way?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on our estimate of the population, it was based on estimates from UNHCR, I -- at this stage I can't go into -- I can't recall all the details, but I'm sure there is a fairly good documentary record for this. And I must say incidentally, and I must say a bit to my surprise, is consistent with that document which Mr. Kehoe submitted which showed 70.000 men in the military-age range or what was very generously described as the military-age range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at least from the percentages you had earlier stated that you expected at most 20 per cent of the population to return to Croatia after Operation Storm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is again the issue I raised earlier, that is what was expected. Let's stick to the figures. From this report I see that by 2000, 41.000, that's at least what the report says, returned, and then out of these 41, that 23.147 returned through the implementation of the programme of return after mid-1998. That means until mid-1998 apparently some 18.000 returned, and in relation to the numbers, the estimates given by Mr. Galbraith, that's 10 percent, and that after the 26th of June, 1998, apparently a higher number returned, that is more than the total number that returned until that moment. That's what the figures tell us. We can -- what percentages are is just a matter of using your calculator. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, nonetheless, not getting into any percentages using the figures that are in this report, this number of people did come back prior to President Tudjman leaving office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report, if it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- and incidentally there is -- it does not mean that all those -- that the 41.141 were people who had been -- who had fled the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it talks about Serbian returnees from Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb Republic of Krajina to their homes in Croatia in general. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I read that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this becomes Exhibit D420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D420 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Next I'd like to call -- by the way, Mr. Ambassador, do you have any information or figures that would -- that would contradict the items in this exhibit that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mandate in Croatia ended on January 3rd, 1998, so it was at a period when there were relatively fewer returns than the total here, as Judge Orie has just pointed out. And, second, I have not meant to suggest that there were no returns. I have meant to testify that Tudjman didn't want any returns, but I have also testified that the United States and European countries put enormous pressure on Croatia to permit returns and so these figures, if they're correct, to my mind simply reflect the great success of American and European diplomacy and so I'm very pleased to see those numbers but that doesn't in any way contradict or diminish my point which is that Tudjman did not want the returns, put every legal barrier in front of it, and in my view permitted the destruction of the Serb property in order to make it impossible for people to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We've heard that, Mr. Galbraith, but that wasn't my question. My question was, do you have any information or figures that would contradict the items, the numbers in this exhibit that we just saw. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, may I point to you that when putting the figures to the witness, you give your own interpretation, for example the period after 26th of June, 1998, until 2000, you're talking about the period when President Tudjman's still was alive. Of course we have no figures on that, and you include in your question suggestions and that confuses me, at least. And I will try to clarify this. Mr. Galbraith, one question in relation to this. It's not a yes or a no question. The programme of return of which I think we have not heard much or anything at all until this moment, do you have any knowledge of how that programme was developed or established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very little, because this took place after I left Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Very little. What do you know, if anything, then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, simply that we had pushed during my time for Croatia to take affirmative action for returns, and I think I knew that there was such a programme. As to the mechanics and the degree of success, I don't know. It was implemented after I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not primarily talking about the content but since you emphasised a couple of times that there was quite some pressure upon Croatia, I wondered if this programme, of which we do not know much or if anything at all, whether this is to be linked in any way to the pressure exercised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it's a 100 percent certain that this is a -- that the pressure that was applied by the United States and European partners was a major factor in Croatia's decision to have this programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know the basis for that last statement. What's the basis for the statement that United States pressure caused Croatia to implement operation return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was a major factor Mr. Galbraith said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was a parliamentary decision, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the United States put enormous pressure on Croatia starting in August 1995, that it had to have a policy in which it permitted the return of all people who were eligible for Croatian citizenship, and meaning in particular Serbs. We did this in the form of public statements by US officials, myself, the secretary of state, the State Department, the press spokesman, I believe that we will find this in statements of President Clinton. We cut off -- we reduced US assistance to Croatia. We cut off certain kinds of aid programmes on this issue. We threatened to cancel the licence for the MPRI contract. We reduced our high-level contacts with Tudjman. We began to isolate him. And all of these things were things that the Croatian government did not want to see happen. And in direct response to our diplomatic initiatives during my time Croatia made changes, directly in response to our demands. Croatia extended the 30-day deadline to 90 days. In response to demands that I presented on behalf of the US government they dropped the 90 days. In a meeting with Ambassador Bill Richardson and myself in Brioni, I think in 1996, President Tudjman issued a statement that we worked out with him, that we -- I would almost say metaphorically twisted his arm to make -- which is that Croatia would permit the return of Serbs. This issue of international and US pressure became so great that in the 2000 election campaign, after Tudjman died, the candidates competed as to who would do the most to facilitate the return of Serbs because they understood that this was a precondition for Croatia's entry -- for Croatia to make progress toward entry into the European Union and into NATO. So I think the record is overwhelming that it was in fact US and European pressure that caused a change in policy from what it was in August of 1995 to the initiation of this programme on return, and -- and to a much more liberal policy after the election of President Mesic in 2000 and the election of a parliament controlled by the opposition in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please pull up 3D00-1212. Now, Mr. Ambassador, you're familiar with the European Court of Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an October 24 2006 decision of the European Court of Human Rights, and it specifically interprets the takeover act which was the act initially which set a proposed deadline of 30 days which was extended to 90 days and which was abolished later in subsequent legislation. If we go to page 3 of this decision, under Section B this case discusses specifically the takeover act, and if we could go full page on the English version, please. Page 3, Section B. Actually, page 3 of the decision, I don't know if it's page three of the document but page 3 of the decision. We're on page 4 of the decision. Now, we need to go -- there we go. Thank you. Highlight the Section B below, please. All right. You were critical of the -- what's called the takeover act, Ambassador Galbraith, and in this case it describes the takeover act as providing the property situated in the previously occupied territories and belonging to persons who had left Croatia should be in the possession and under the control of the state, meaning the state of Croatia, and that act also provided and allowed for persons who were displaced from other areas to use those abandoned properties for lack of a better term, during the absence of the owners of those properties. And if those owners wanted the properties back, they would have filed a request for repossession with the competent local authority. On the second page -- or page 4, if we go to page 4, this act also provided that "the ministry shall compensate the damage suffered by the owner who has submitted a request for repossession of his property prior to 30 October 2002 but to whom the property has not been returned by that date." Now, the complaint in this case claimed that this takeover act and its amendments were "aimed at preventing people of Serbian origin from returning to their homes in Croatia." If we go to page 6 of this decision, second paragraph, it says: "As to the conduct of the administrative authorities in ensuring the repossession of the house in question to the applicant, the Court observes, firstly, that the state," meaning Croatia, "had a legitimate interest in housing displaced persons in the property left behind by persons who left Croatia during the war. Furthermore, the system which allows such persons to remain in the occupied property before they have been provided with adequate housing, is not in itself in contradictions with the guarantees contained in Article 1 of Protocol 1 ..." In -- two paragraphs later there is a discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I read the rest it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you stopped reading. It says: "Providing that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Providing that it ensures sufficient safeguards for the protection of applicants's property rights. In this respect it is crucial to note that the applicant has never instituted any proceedings for compensation in respect of the use of his house by occupants placed there by the state authorities." And there is a discussion two paragraphs later about how the proceedings in Croatia were not unnecessarily long under the circumstances. And then -- on the next page, the court ends up dismissing the claim because the applicant didn't seek the enforcement order to be carried out, didn't seek compensation, and that the national judicial authorities did not show that there was any issue to be considered by the Court as a violation of the protocol. Now, this is just one of the cases involved in interpreting the takeover act. Now are you critical of the takeover act but at least in this case the European Court of human rights does not grant any sort of judgement or give any sort of remedy to the applicant for a violation, does it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, before I would wish to comment on this, naturally I would wanted to read the entire case and the entire decision. But I can say in superficially looking at this document, a few points. First, it refers to the takeover act and the amendments made in 2002. I have no idea what those amendments are or how they affected it. Second, this concerned proceedings that were initiated, as best I can tell, again, from the very superficial chance I have had a chance to look at this, proceedings initiated in 2003. I have already testified that after Tudjman died and after Mesic became president and after Racan became prime minister that Croatia had a 180-degree turn on this issue. And so I can completely understand that the European court might find proceedings that were undertaken in 2003 at a time when there was a different government and a different attitude, did not violate the relevant human rights statutes. What I was testifying to was the takeover act and actions as applied in 1995. And at that time the plan, Tudjman's plan, was to confiscate property after 30 days unless people returned and he did everything possible to make it physically impossible for people to return. Furthermore in that period, when some people did return and did try to recover their property, the court proceedings and procedures were structured -- and local authorities were structured in a way and acted in a way that made it impossible for people to return to recover their property. And so it was in that period, 1995, 1996, 1997, the laws were not administered -- there was no justice there was effectively -- it was very difficult, if not impossible for people to recover their property and in numerous trips I made to the Krajina region I talked to people who could not get their property back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I haven't done so I would like to move to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However, Mr. Kuzmanovic, usually decisions by courts are not introduced into evidence. I have no problem with it, but if all the case law will be tendered as evidence this is public decision by a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a couple --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do not, if you think it assists us, of having it in evidence rather than to, as we usually do, just to consult the case law. Our attention has been drawn to it and it saves half a wood, if we would refrain from that, so I ask you whether you still persist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what I will do is I'll refer to the cases so the court will know and I won't need to tender them if I refer to the specific cases involved because I have a couple of other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you -- then please proceed and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before can he get on to the next case, Mr. Galbraith, I'd like the registrar to pull up 65 ter 00956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps already for the record this is a decision of the European Court on Human Rights, first section, application number 35670-03 the case of Ceratlic [phoen] against Croatia dated the 24th October 2006. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the decree that you were critical of, which was promulgated on the 31st of August, 1995. It is a decree on the temporary takeover on administration of certain properties. Article 10, which is on page 4, provides for the 30-day time period that you are critical of. I'd like to you take a moment and read this document and please tell me where in this document you find the words "confiscation" or "stripping persons of Serb nationality of their citizenship," and feel free to take your time to take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties agree on whether these words appear in this document or not. I mean, apart from that I would be highly surprised to find such language at all in such kind of decisions, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Galbraith --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we really ask Mr. Galbraith to read this whole document to find out the words, as you just explained, and do not appear in this document, because that's what you're inviting him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me, Mr. Galbraith, that the words confiscation of property and stripping persons of Serbian nationality of citizenship are not contained in this decree, are they?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to read the decree you will have to provided me the entire decree and I will read it and tell you whether those words appear or not, but I'm not going to agree or disagree if I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If the Prosecutor is willing to stipulate to that we'll stipulate, otherwise we'll have Mr. Galbraith read the document. It is a little more than four pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately I'm not in a position to do anything more than the court in this instance; and that is to say, I would also be surprised if that precise language appeared in there, but I wouldn't be candid if I suggested that I could say with certainty that -- none of those words appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the testimony was that Mr. Galbraith said this decree was the -- provides for the confiscation of Serbian property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a different matter, Mr. Kuzmanovic, isn't it. Whether that same words appear in the document, that's totally different question. I mean, when you summarize the gist of a document you don't necessarily use the exactly same words as you find in the document. I mean, this is a useless exercise. I take it of course if you insist, I will read all the four pages and then see whether these words appear. Again, I would be highly surprised. Let's go to the core of what the evidence is. If there are certain portions of this document where you say, No. You see that that is not what the document says, then please do so. But let's not enter into a semantic discussion. Please proceed. Again, I do not oppose at all against looking at this document, but let's do it by such questions that assist the Chamber and that's not whether exactly these words appear and that was your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well the statement was that the government passed a decree that provided for the confiscation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, of course, I explained it to you, if you didn't get it, then just perhaps follow my guidance that could you go to what really is the issue at stake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the discussion of the Croatian parliament was in relation to this decree, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't now recall what the discussion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know what the law is, what is the basis that you have for making the claim that it confiscates property?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me restate this. The effect of this decree was to confiscate property that -- and of Croatian actions was to confiscate property of people who did not return in 30 days and then it would be settled, the plan was that this would then be settled as part of the overall settlement of claims between Croatia and Yugoslavia, in which these -- these Croatian citizens who, in Tudjman's words were optansi, had opted out the Croatia by the act of fleeing, their property claims would be settled as part of an overall settlement which, in effect, would give them nothing. Our view was that what Croatia was trying to do was to confiscate the property of Serbs who had left and that Croatia was making it impossible for those people to return to claim their property by having a short deadline. We didn't think any deadline would apply or should apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what is what ended up happening --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of our pressure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what ended up happening in early 1996 was that there ended up being no deadline. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of United States pressure, yes, that was the end result. I consider that a success of our diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask you whether it was because of the United States pressure, did I?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed you that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The amendment, first amendment in September of 1995, 65 ter 3497, extended that deadline which was a decree, I'll rephrase the question. The law which was passed in September of 1995, which was 65 ter 3497, was the parliament's law. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- yes, that's how laws are passed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the parliament opted for a deadline different from what the government decree was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tudjman's party controlled the parliament. It was a pliant institution of Tudjman. So the change in date was a change that the Tudjman government made and that the parliament enacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Article 11 of the document, 65 ter 3497, provides the 90-day extension. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I mean, I would have to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to Article 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that in the second sentence it provides for the 90 days. "From the date of the entering of this law into force."

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me please read this. Can we see Article 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Article five provides for the temporary possession for displaced persons and refugees in those abandoned properties. And those people would eventually, the people meaning the owners, would eventually have a right to have those people evicted when they came back to claim the properties.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, it would appear, although I would have to read the whole document, but I will accept the premise of your question, that the -- the Article 11 does change the date from 30 days to 90 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender 65 ter 00956 and 03497.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 00956 becomes Exhibit D421. 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter 03497 become Exhibit D422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D421 and D422 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
