utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, please pull up 65 ter 00781.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you will take a look, this is an amendment in January of 1996, to Article 11, which puts it in line with the agreement on normalisation of relations between Croatia and Yugoslavia. And at least the change eliminates any deadline within this particular law.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to make clear that this does not put it in line with the agreement of normalisation because this is six months before the agreement on normalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "It will be regulated." Meaning that -- in the future.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well ... I can't see how it could be regulated by an agreement that doesn't yet exist. Perhaps regulated by a agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nonetheless, 65 ter 3059 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If could you pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This act of parliament rescinds the law on temporary confiscation and control, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the title says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a decision -- before I get into that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender 65 ter 00781 and 3059.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 00781 becomes Exhibit D423 and 65 ter 03059 becomes Exhibit number D424.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D423 and D424 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of a constitutional court decision in September of 1997, a Croatian constitutional court decision, in which it upheld the takeover law but eliminated the deadline and added a compensation aspect to the law?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm sure I was aware of the decision in 1997. In 2008 my memory of it is a little vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you please pull up 3D00-1203. Just for reference I think it should be 3D00-1203 I think -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I have only taken out excerpts in the translation of the entire document, Mr. Galbraith. But you can see there's a discussion of Article 11 in the second paragraph -- fourth paragraph which would be page 6 of the original. And that the court deems portions of the law unconstitutional. And if you go to the second page of the translation, if you're still reading just let me know and I will let you read through.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just read that paragraph. Did you want me to read the whole page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Only if you need to, otherwise I'll direct your attention to the second page. I don't want to prevent you from reading anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. Kuzmanovic, read it if you need to read it is a rather confusing instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure he doesn't want to read it and I probably wouldn't want to read it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll go to the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, it discusses the fact that Article 11, subsection 1 of the disputed laws determines that the question of returning into possession and usage of property will be regulated by the agreement on normalisation of relations between Croatia and Yugoslavia. Is it your recollection there was no such agreement in 1997, at this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- I previously testified that in January of 1996 there wasn't such agreement but we've already looked at a document which I believe was from the summer of 1996 on the normalization of relations. I'd like to make a point, though, about this, which is that our view was that the right of Croatian citizens to their property in -- was -- was and could in no way be regulated by an agreement between Croatia and Yugoslavia. That to view this as something that fell within the jurisdiction of Yugoslavia was -- was not -- I mean, and this was an excuse that the Croatian authorities used with us, but in our view the rights of these people should have fallen strictly within the rubric of the Croatian constitution and European human rights standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you've got the decision with respect to no deadline, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the no deadline came from January of 1996, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And you've got an extension in this particular constitutional court decision which basically says you can't, as we say in American parlance, there is no taking without just compensation, meaning that they provide for a mechanism to be reimbursed for their property in this constitutional court decision, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue on -- on compensation, what we felt that people should have the right to recover their property and if the property had been damaged, then have the same right to compensation that other people had, particularly Croats, had to get assistance or compensation for a property that might be damaged. We did not believe that compensation was an appropriate response in a case where the property had been taken and given to somebody else. And, incidentally, it wasn't just a displaced people, that is, people who had been displaced from the fighting in 1991 who had been given this property. Tudjman was inviting Croats from the diaspora. He was hoping they would come from Australia to come and live in Krajina. There was a real effort to change the population of the Krajina, that had nothing to do with housing displaced people. And the idea that people would be paid for property because it had been taken to give to somebody else we thought that was unacceptable and a violation of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the decision doesn't state that whoever temporarily occupied the property would be able to stay there and that they would just pay off the owner as a result. The law contemplated, did it not, at least as it is written, that people who were temporarily occupying those properties would be potentially evicted, the people who wanted their properties back would get them back, and if there was damage to the property or if there was property that was being used by that particular temporary occupant the owner should be compensated for it. Do you know that? I don't want to try and trick you.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I would have to read through all these documents. Again, the scheme that, really, have I been focussed on, was the initial scheme, which was to confiscate the property that belonged to the optansi [phoen] and after 30 days and extend it to 90 days, and that would be the end of the story with those people compensated as part of this bilateral agreement between Croatia and Yugoslavia. Eventually these legal impediments were made less severe and eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have 3D00-1223 tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is becomes Exhibit D425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D425 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now the issue of refugees, for example, of placing refugees in abandoned properties, Croatia was facing at least at that time in August of 1995, a significant refugee crisis, was it not? Even after the Serbs of the Krajina had left, there were Croats coming in from Banja Luka and in -- from other areas that were being pushed out as a result of the ongoing fighting, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some additional refugees, but by and large the Croat refugees' problem was one that had taken place earlier. Obviously in Croatia in 1991 and people from -- in Bosnia earlier in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please pull up 1D -- that's 1D33-0105.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And before we get into the document, Ambassador, while it's coming up, would you agree with me that post-Operation Storm roughly about 80 per cent of the people who may have owned property in Sectors North and South would have fled and abandoned their property?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, in some sense the figure would have been much higher if you included Croats who been expelled in 1991, but because, as you know, many of the people who owned property in Sectors North and South were Croat, but if you want to talk about just the Serb -- Serb-owned property, 80 per cent or maybe a higher figure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless it was a substantial number of people?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh very substantial. 80 per cent I think would be low.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a transcript of a government of Croatia meeting of the 23rd of August which discusses this decree and eventual law, and I'd like to direct your attention to -- my pages are not numbered, unfortunately, so let me count them off from the front page. It's page 7 of the English version, which includes the cover page. That's it. And this is a discussion, and I'll refer you to the centre of the document, in the -- the long paragraph that starts: "I think Mr. Prime minister..." If we could go about a third of the way down, the sentence on the right begins: "One of the ..." It is it blocked off on the screen. There you go. Can we enlarge that, please, so it can be readable. Thank you. We'll start, if can enlarge this section, there we go. The discussion is -- is about the temporary accommodation of returns and it says: "One of the important and most important tasks right now is the temporary accommodation of the returnees regardless of whether they are our returnees or the displaced persons from our neighbour country, Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I will skip the next sentence. "From all these conclusions it is evident that the most important thing is to maximally coordinate the civilian authorities, the military, and the police in securing persons and property and in this respect the county prefects shall have the obligation to cooperate with the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Interior as regards the establishment of joint control in these areas, including any passing check-points." utterances.text: Yes. And in that sense it is a very dramatic change from Tudjman's view that is correct these were optansi, opted out from Croatia, and not entitled to return from three years earlier.

utterances.text: And this is June of 1998 when President Tudjman was still president of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were people in that category, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, their leadership made it pretty clear that they didn't want to live in a Republic of Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of Milan Babic, I think the answer to that question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The issue pertaining to people who had left, would you agree with me that the people who lived in that part of Croatia before they left, all voted or the majority of them voted in a referendum to form the RSK, and become a separate entity apart from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it is pretty safe to say, is it not, that the people who did not want to live in a -- the Republic of Croatia didn't care what kind of laws there were or whether they would get their property back, they simply didn't want to live in the Republic of Croatia under any circumstances?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. I think that they cared deeply that they get their property back. Many of them -- I mean this was something that was valuable. Also, how people felt in 1995 in a time of war was going to be different, and we understood this, from how they might feel in 1998 or years later, and it may that be those people would reconsider and decide that in fact, yes, they wanted to live in Croatia, especially we didn't think that the Tudjman government and the kind of nationalism that it represented was going to last forever. utterances.text: As a matter of fact the Tudjman government brought about this act of parliament for the return and care of expelled persons, refugees a displaced persons, did it not, in June 1998?

utterances.text: The procedural history continues on the third page. And if we go to page 6 in the middle of the page where it says: "In 1998 parliament adopted," meaning the Croatian parliament, "a programme for return of refugees and displaced persons which guaranteed the return of their possessions to persons who had left Croatia. However, temporary occupiers were to be placed at a state-owned accommodation." And that "the government argued this programme was adopted in order to protect public interest; namely, to secure repossession of property to persons who had left Croatia and whose property had been given for temporary use to other persons but at the same time to protect refugees who were placed in houses owned by the previous group of persons." Now, if we go to the last page, page 7, this particular applicant in section 2 complained that he was discriminated against on the basis of his Serbian origin alleging that no single eviction order this had been carried out in the Petrinja area where the owner of the house was a person of Serbian origin. In the paragraph following the indented quote, the government of Croatia had provided statistics that there had been such proceedings and that the court noted a little further down, meaning the Court of European -- the European Court of Human Rights noted that "the programme for return equally applies all person who return to Croatia irrespective of their ethnic origin and that there is no indication that the applicant was discriminated against in any respect." Now, the programme of return in 1998 was the start, was it not, of a more -- maybe not necessarily efficient but at least a more procedural manner of trying to get people back in Croatia, was it not.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The start -- the start of a more procedural manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a confusing question. This case, specifically the Kostic case, notes that this particular programme is not discriminatory in its application, meaning that applies equally to all citizens meaning that this person in this particular case who was of Serb origin was not discriminated against. Would you agree me that this 1998 law better streamlined and gave Serbia -- citizens of -- Croatians citizens of Serb nationality a much better opportunity to return to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I will agree with you that it gave Serb -- Croatian citizens of Serb nationality better opportunities to return to Croatia and that is very much consistent with my testimony, that things got better. Without looking at the law and -- and going through it and going through these cases, I can't -- I don't feel I can testify as to whether it is streamlined procedures or did other things, but I would say that it -- it did make things better.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I get to ask the questions here, so ...

utterances.text: Well I -- I can't speak to what was motivating the constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess maybe we could take them one at a time. American pressure didn't influence the constitutional court's decision in that regard, is that pretty clear?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any American pressure on the constitutional court of Croatia to come down with this decision?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was very significant American pressure on Croatia. That pressure was covered in the newspapers. It was known in government circles. And whether it influenced the thinking of the court, I can't say. What I can say is that the way -- what we stressed and we were joined with our European allies, we stressed fundamental principles of human rights as well as treaty obligations that Croatia had, and courts often do think about human rights treaties, they do think about human rights standards, so I can't say whether that influenced the court decision or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not President Tudjman had any influence one way or the other on the Croatian constitutional court, from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my recollection, and I -- I may not be entirely correct on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to you guess but ...

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the court was a institution, as I recall, that was set up as part of the constitutional structure of Croatia which was controlled by Tudjman's party, so I would guess that he had probably had some influence on who became judges and their views. I don't think we thought of the Croatian judiciary as a completely independent institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, compared to the -- the United States did stress makes the same kind of pressures and arguments -- maybe not necessarily you, but the government on Serbia, with regard to human rights issues on a frequent basis in that time-frame, did it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of success rate did you have with them compared to what you had with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had very substantially more influence on Croatia than we did on Serbia, because -- well, because, first, Croatia had been very dependant on the United States for the events that led to the recovery of the occupied territory, the -- the Erdut Agreement, the end of the Muslim-Croat war, because Tudjman and the Croatian people saw that their future was linked to the west, and they wanted the support of the United States for Croatia to become part of -- well, eventually of NATO and the European Union. And Serbia had fewer of those ambitions. The United States had imposed sanctions on Serbia along with the rest of the United Nations. It had used air power against Serbia -- or Bosnian-Serb forces in 1994 and 1995, and then, of course, you had the build up to the Kosovo war in 1999. So very different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you had said that Croatia had become fairly dependant on the United States in many instances for what had transpired during that time-frame. utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Operation Storm and the subsequent campaign in Bosnia was -- was critical to arriving at the Dayton peace agreements. But, no. I would not say that the United States was dependant on Croatia. This was not a vital interest to -- an area of vital interest to the United States. Our national survival did not depend on it. We very much wanted to end the war, and we saw that Croatia was the key to ending the war, and this really goes back to 1993 when we began to work to negotiate an end to the Muslim-Croat war to create the Federation. We saw that Croatia in this three conflict that Croatia had the swing role, and I think it was a success of our diplomacy that we got Croatia and the Bosnian government on the same side, and we got Croatia to set aside some of Tudjman's more nationalist impulses to bring about a positive result. But I do not believe that the United States was dependent on Croatia on the same way that Croatia was dependent on the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me that the Croatian military was the military that undertook this undertaking, not NATO, not the American military, not the UN, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, NATO began a major bombing campaign on the 30th of August, 1995, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia though, right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what -- and it was in that period that the Croatian army and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina made the major military advances. NATO was not the Federation air force. That wasn't the role. The bombing was a response to the Sarajevo marketplace massacre, but it had the effect of -- of inflicting great damage on the Bosnian-Serb military and particularly on the command and control, and then there were forces on the ground that were able to take advantage of it.

utterances.text: With what happened at Varivode?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I was at the time, and we raised this issue in a very strong way with the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look on page 8 or, actually, of the partial draft of the translation, at least in terms of the summary, and I will give you the 3D number on the bottom right. It is 0696. And before I get to the actual transcript, I'll just give you a little synopsis of what the transcript is about so you can get some context, Mr. Ambassador. Here the minister of internal affairs is reporting about this incident, and on the measures taken by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, after a discussion which took place which was led by Prime Minister Valentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move -- well, D214 is already in. We'll go to D215. And we'll go to 0681.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I will stress there was a closed session. So there is no public hearing, there is no newspapers to see, there is no grandstanding in front of the television cameras here, to give you the context. This is a closed meeting within the parliament of these particular people that were listed in the agenda. The paragraph above the prime minister is Mr. Jarnjak talking at the end of essentially that he hopes in a few days: "We will have information. So very soon we will be able to publicly release the names of the persons who even perpetrated this act." So he is basically advising the group present about what he is doing, and the prime minister of Croatia talks on the following few pages, and I think it is very important, given the fact that is a closed session --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, just before we leave that page I noted that an aspect of the paragraph above the one that was read out bears on a comment made earlier by the witness in connection with -- with the Varivode incident, and I thought it might be helpful for the witness to see it or for it to be read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Relates to the accusations made by the Croatian Helsinki Committee regarding this incident. And perhaps the politization one way or the other of what was going on in Varivode in relation to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the just before what you read is actually more relevant, which is "I'm saying The pressure from the public, from the international public on all sides is exceptionally great, and this is an attempt. We released a statement on yesterday -- on Monday, we released a statement yesterday, renewing the statement given a broad response to the accusations made by the Croatian Helsinki Committee because this is now certainly conducive to this climate and the election campaign activities which have commenced. And everybody is trying to transform this to suit their own sphere of influence of interest." That's a little hard to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's our experience, Mr. Galbraith, that once you start reading, speed of speech goes up. The translation has caught up. Please proceed, where I invite you to slow down or to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that statement is a little confusing to understand, but I think what's important here and what is very consistent with my observations is that phrase, "I am saying the pressure from the international public on all sides is exceptionally great." That was their concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see what the prime minister's discussion in the bottom of that page and in the following page says. At the bottom of the page, the prime minister talks about, and I will start in the middle: "But above all I want to say here for the sake of the minutes and for the sake of my own accountability, a state in which civilians are killed regardless of whom is in question, thus the state cannot intervene ... " And we'll go to the next page. "Where it cannot protect civilians, that state has no chance of achieving those objectives for which we are fighting. I understand entirely that there is a little of everything, vengeance, and greed, and violence, but we have to accord the greatest importance to this. I spoke about this with the utmost gravity with the president of the country who is the only one with the possibility because he has authority over the army's Chief of Staff where the government has no normal nor de facto, for that matter, authority, so I therefore personally, and I will say this on every occasion, I will not remain at ease as a person until we find this perpetrator and until he is punished. "This is significant to everyone who lives in this state. Nobody can kill anybody, particularly not innocent elderly people, and for this to be on behalf of higher purposes. There are no higher purposes for which this may be considered justified, but this cannot by any means be simply forgotten. Another important thing to say, events of this nature cause great damage to us, political and economic. Croatia cannot join the council of Europe. There is no integration into international financial institutions. Those of you now going to Washington will see - tomorrow I am going to Warsaw - the type of questions and pressures with which we will be confronted here -- there." The statement goes on in very strong language on the rest of this page and continues into the next page, if we could go to the next page. At the last paragraph. He ends with - that's Prime Minister Valentic - ends with: "Therefore, this is very serious. And I am telling you my views as a person and as the prime minister, and I repeat that I am aware that in a such a horrible situation in which hundreds of thousands of people are displaced, refugees, and killed that all kinds of things happen. But it is the test of the state -- but the test of the state lies in the fact of whether we can stop this or not. To speak of a market economy, to speak of democracy where people are killed, ladies and gentlemen, this simply does not exist. Let us introduce military administration, police administration there, anything, let us set up camps, put up barbed wire, but we cannot have cowboys going around and killing people." Now that sounds like something you would have said, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could have said it as eloquently as Prime Minister Valentic said it, but I've testified before on this point but I will repeat it. There were many decent people in the government of Croatia who did not like what was going on. I already spoke about Foreign Minister Granic. I didn't interact as much with Valentic, but clearly it is a sing of -- strong statement from him and a sign that he was a person of integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the tone of this discussion, given in a closed session, by the prime minister of the country, sound to you like this was a government that had no desire to prevent this sort of thing from occurring?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people in the government who did not want this to occur, but I think I have to call your attention to something that Prime Minister Valentic said earlier in that statement, and if you go back to the previous page, I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Yes, near the top regarding the president.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that -- yes. "I spoke with utmost gravity with the president of the country who is the only one with the possibility because he has the authority over the army's Chief of Staff where the government," the government meaning the prime minister and his cabinet, "has no formal nor de facto for that matter authority." And under the Croatian system as it existed under Tudjman, the president was in charge of national security and of the Ministry of Defence and foreign affair, not the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that not just Prime Minister Valentic and Foreign Minister Granic that there were significant numbers of people within the Croatian government that detested this and wanted to have it stopped at all possible costs?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were others, absolutely. And I think you see this. This is one reason why I believe our pressure was effective because we actually had allies within the Croatian government, among the Croatian public, among the non-governmental organisations, and I think the Croatian people, and you see this very clearly in 2000 when the elections took place and they voted overwhelmingly for a president and prime minister who made possible the returns that we looked at in that paragraph chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a very short video-clip, Mr. Ambassador. It is probably less than 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an transcript. It is two people and it is about four lines and the booth does have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This particular snippet was a snippet from General Mladic who talked about the potential of what would happen at Bihac, similar to what happened at Srebrenica and Zepa, and that was a very real fear and you've talked about that fear, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very real fear. Seeing him gives me a certain chill to think about what would have happened had he succeeded in taking Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour I would like to move that short snippet into evidence. It's 3D00-1356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic the text does not appear in the transcript. It just says "videotape played." These were only a couple of lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were four lines. Why don't we just play it again, Your Honour, and maybe hopefully it will get picked up in the transcript. It is short enough for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the booth work with the transcript provided and the transcript reflect the English translation of the words spoken by the persons appearing in the individual. Could we play it again, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "REPORTER: Mr. General, will the Muslims from Bihac continue to provoke the Serb defence in the area of Ribic and there on much longer? "RATKO MLADIC: Yes, they will until they have been completely defeated as they were in Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that remedy it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noted that we have it now on the transcript, question and answer. I heard it being translated into French as well and I think the original is on the audio. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador were you aware of an operation that the ARSK was going to conduct in conjunction with the Bosnian Serb army called Operation Mac during this time-frame?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The code-name right now doesn't -- I can't think of what it was, but I knew that the ARSK and the Bosnian Serb army were together attacking Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just like Your Honour -- we have -- go ahead counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just notice that after Mr. Kuzmanovic moved the snippet of the video into evidence, the concern was raised about the translation, so it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- never connected that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me, Mr. Tieger. May I take it that this is to say that you have no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that's completely correct. That looks like the same video we have seen before. I just want to confirm that we have it in its entirety and can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the snippet shown in opening statement that the Gotovina had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we have -- it looks like the same interview that was shown in other contacts, so as long as we have the entire interview, I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you do have the entire interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the entire interview in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I think we've seen various clips from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Various clips, separate portions. Then Mr. Registrar, this part would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D430.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D430 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to call up a document regarding Operation Mac, 3D00-0773. And we've asked for this document to be translated into English, Your Honour, quite some time ago. It has not been translated and I was going to ask my counsel -- my colleague Goran to read just a portion of this document in Croatian, and it will be translated and then I will ask Mr. Galbraith a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it is it not the task for the interpreters to provide translations, but if very small portions are read that doesn't meet usually such objections that we couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is small, Your Honour, and we put in for a while ago, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull that document up, too so it could be followed along even despite it's only a B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this document is an information from the main headquarters of the Republika Srpska army department of security, and it has been titled as realisation of the task from the operative action called Mac, which means Sword 1, and I will seed it in original, just a small portion of this document. It says like this: [Interpretation] "In the beginning of the month of July this year, the command of the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina wrote a directive on the execution of Operation Mac, Sword, which relates to active operations against the 5th Corps with the objective of crushing it completely. "Operation Sword should have, according to plan, begun on the 15th of July, year 1995 as is meant in the title, in the early morning hours. The operation engages the forces of the Command Pauk, as well as parts of the forces of the 21st and 39th Corps. In the framework of this operation (during preparations), the commander of the Serbian army of Krajina decided to use biological means, namely the method of poisoning consumer articles, (flour, sugar, oil, liquid detergents for dish-washing), and sell in illegal trade these to the 5th Corps, thus causing massive disease among fighting men and disabling them. Incubation lasts from five to seven days," I'm reading a footnote, "a normal dose has been tested on the illegal -- illegally defected member of the Ustasha, Goran Marijanovic, by injecting into a liquid meal of which humanitarian international organisations knew nothing. Within three days the above mentioned symptoms occurred that lasted six days. Medical assistance was given to him which probably shortened the duration of the response. "This pharmaceutical is in the form of powder produced in Republika Srpska. If taken in larger quantities and depending on the resistance powers of a particular individual, they can cause death. Otherwise, the side effects of normal use are stomach conditions, diarrhea, headache, and stomach cramps. As of the 22nd July 1995 we have not registered any cases of disease. Securing these articles for sale to the 5th Corps and injecting them into food in order -- and other articles in order to disable manpower was done by the intelligence centre from the intelligence administration of the Main Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, located in Topusko, in which -- which action involved Colonel Nikola Zimonja and Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Krgovic. Also engaged was a self-employed businessman, Nenad Misevic from Glina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks for your patience in listening to that, ambassador. Does this particular Operation Mac, does that refresh your recollection at all as to whether or not you knew -- had any idea of that operation being contemplated by the joint Bosnian-Serb RSK?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did know about a -- as I testified on a number of points about a joint operation of the army ARSK and the Bosnian-Serb army intended to take Bihac, which is obviously the same as what we're talking about here when they speak of crushing the 5th Corps. Now as to the other part of this document which relates to trying to poison the 5th Corps, of that I had no information, at least as best I can recall and it is pretty dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move that -- tender that document into evidence please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can MFI that if necessary... [Overlapping speakers] translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's probably more prudent, but I'm at Court's disposal for that. I think -- sorry I'm looking at the translation which I don't think corresponds to this. But again, in general, no objection, but if it is going to be independently translated then I suppose that should be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Kuzmanovic, what now happened is a part from a small portion of crushing the 5th Corps, that we get a long story about the use of poison, where the witness says, I have got no idea about it. That is of course not an appropriate way of proceeding. You should have asked the witness first, in relation to such an operation, were you aware of any reports about poison being used to eliminate opponents and you might have given one or two details in order to refresh his memory, but now it becomes a demonstration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, had I had the translation that's probably what I would have done and I apologies for taking up a little bit more time than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only about time, Mr. Kuzmanovic. I think that you understand. I'm not blaming you for taking two minutes. I'm blaming you for reading a long story about horrible things intended where the witness says, I've got no idea, and you should have first explored whether we could expect any evidence of this witness on these matters. Otherwise, it is just a demonstration and which we have seen more in this case that we get a long explanation on who was successful in what -- who was horrible person, horrible units. I'm not talking about one party or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will keep that in mind Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's try not to create devils and angles whoever the devils and angels may have been apart from focussing on the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is not by the way addressed just to you but is addressed to all the parties, Prosecution and all Defence parties. And Mr. Kuzmanovic, I'm looking at the clock and I see that we have two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm on my last section, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your on your last section, how much time will that take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe five extra minutes if they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five extra minutes. I will risk the blame by my colleague who supposed to sit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Blame me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't help, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the offer anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you had said that these attacks on Bihac in large part were occurring from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I said that they occurred from the territory of the Republic of Croatia but I -- I -- as I recall, most of the attacks on Bihac were by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Nonetheless the Croatian territory was being used in part to attack Bihac. Correct? At the safe area of Bihac? Because as you said Croatia had obligation to prevent attacks from its territory and --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answered your question with yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And Mrksic, of course, was a JNA general who was using Sector South in conjunction with Mladic in and around Bihac, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mrksic was the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mrksic was the commander of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina who was installed by Milosevic and there therefore was in command of the ARSK forces that were attacking Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I wanted to ask you just a couple of other questions relating to Bihac, specifically related to the UN presence in Sector South. General Forand was the commander of Sector South based there Knin, we you aware of that, Canadian general?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: He testified here a few weeks ago and at various points in his transcript on page 4401, lines 10 to 17, and 4402, and 03, lines 20 to 25 and line 1, and I cite that for the benefit of the record, he was unaware that Bihac was an UN safe area. The question I wanted to ask you was: You dealt extensively with the UN over the course of time you were ambassador in Croatia, can you explain how it was possible if you know that the commander of Sector South does not know that Bihac is a protected area?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is difficult to -- sorry Your Honour, difficult to imagine how that kind of inquiry is anything other than speculative and can assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If he doesn't know, he can tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was listening to the French translation so just catch up. Yes, the question what are you going at, the reference to a lot of transcript pages, and then the question I do not see. But if you understood the question, if you can simply answer that question, Mr. Galbraith, you're invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can say is that I would be very surprised and dismayed, to be honest, if the commanding general of the UN forces did not know that Bihac was a safe area. But I can't answer your question as to how it is -- as to, first, whether he didn't know, because I don't know, and how it's possible that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The last area I'd like to talk to you about or the last question would be -- would you agree with me that, in terms of the overall solution to the problem, both in Croatia and in Bosnia, Croatia became part of the solution and was not part of the problem?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia was a victim, in 1991, in became part of the problem in 1993, it became part of the solution in 1995 and then became part of the problem in the immediate aftermath of military operations and eventually in the late 1990s and certainly after the change of government in 2000 has been very much a part of the solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, did we get a D number for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we get a D number for that, we get a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D number but it should be MFIed for the time being because there is no translation yet and Mr. Tieger has not finally taken position. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document 3D00-1310 and it becomes Exhibit D341 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could you give us an indication, Mr. Tieger, and since I know Mr. Galbraith is listening as well, how much time you need to re-examine the witness in taking that still the Cermak Defence has no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we certainly finish in the -- unless the Court would have extensive questions we would finish in the first session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First session is re-examination or the whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I would not need all of that, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm estimating 45 minutes to an hour right now, but I'll work on that this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Over night the need for time grows, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, it can go in either direction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's good. Could I get an indication from the Defence teams. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Naturally, if there is any further commentary on redirect examination, that would be all we would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is difficult to give an estimate --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The same Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same. At least, Mr. Galbraith, this could make you confident that we'll finish tomorrow, hopefully not too late in the morning, because we'll -- we will adjourn, but not until after I have instructed you not to speak with anyone about the testimony whether already given or still to be given. And we adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 and I think it's Courtroom II, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Registrar is nodding yes. So it is Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
